subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Less Is More Effects
description: One-minute skill: Less Is More Effects.

hook.text: Heart attack diagnosis: a simple 3-question tree beat a complex logistic regression in the emergency room.

buildup.text: More data and more variables can actually reduce prediction accuracy in uncertain environments.

discovery.text: Less-is-more: simple models avoid overfitting. They capture the signal and ignore the noise.

twist.text: Complex models memorize the training data's quirks. Simple models capture the underlying pattern. Simplicity transfers.

climax.text: In unpredictable environments, the best strategy is often the simplest one that captures the key cue.

punchline.text: More data can mean more noise. Simplify.

quiz.question: Why can simpler models outperform complex ones?
options: Simple models avoid overfitting to noise

details.summary: Less-is-more effects occur when using less information, fewer cues, or simpler models produces better predictions than using more. In uncertain environments, additional information introduces noise that degrades prediction quality rather than improving it.
details.whyItMatters: Less-is-more challenges the common assumption that more data always helps. In many real-world environments, complex models overfit to noise while simple models capture the essential signal. This is practically important for data-driven organizations.
takeaways: More information can decrease prediction accuracy in noisy environments
Simple models outperform complex ones when the sample is small or noise is high
The benefit of additional information depends on the environment's structure

faq.question: When does more information hurt decision quality?
faq.answer: When the environment is noisy and unpredictable, when the sample size is small relative to the number of variables, and when the additional information has low validity. In these conditions, extra data adds noise faster than signal.

faq.question: How is the less-is-more effect related to overfitting?
faq.answer: Complex models with many parameters fit training data perfectly, including its noise. When applied to new data, the noise-fitting hurts predictions. Simpler models with fewer parameters miss some patterns but are robust to noise, producing better out-of-sample predictions.
